title: The End of Reading Is Not the End of Thinking
subtitle: We are losing a faculty. It may not be the one we think.
description: We are losing a faculty. It may not be the one we think.
body_html:
We may be the last generation that reads. That is not a slogan; it is close to what the numbers describe. In the early 1990s about six in ten American adults read a book for pleasure in a given year. By 2022 it was under half. Daily reading for pleasure fell from more than a quarter of adults to about one in six in under two decades, and more than a quarter of adults now read at the lowest measured level, able to take in a short passage but not to hold a long argument or draw an inference from it. There is a name for where this points. People have started calling it the slide toward a post-literate society, one that still takes in information, through video, through summaries, through clips and feeds and the explanations a machine will generate on request, but that takes it in less and less through reading.

The fear underneath the numbers is not really about books. It is about thought. Reading, the argument goes, is where a mind learns to do its hardest work: to hold an idea across time, to carry a through-line, to build an argument and feel for the place where it is weak. If reading is dying, then the thinking that reading built is dying with it. We are not losing a pastime. We are losing a faculty.

I take that fear seriously. I am just no longer sure it describes what I actually live.

Because the most honest thinking I do all week does not happen with a book in my hands. It happens at the gym, with a weight in my hand and a voice in my ear. I work at a screen all day, and the one stretch of time when I am reliably alone with my own mind is the hour when I am reading nothing at all. I am listening. And somewhere between the third set and the walk back to the car, something I heard days ago finally turns over and shows me a side of itself I had not seen.

Two faculties, not one

When I listen like that, I am not doing what reading does, and I know it. Reading is the slow, exacting faculty. It moves line by line, catches the weak joint in a sentence, holds the argument to account. Listening opens a different one. I am not tracking every line; I am pondering the whole, feeling for the common thread, thinking into a thing rather than through it. It is looser and more contemplative, and it does a kind of work my careful reading never gets to. A second place of processing is how it feels from the inside.

The tradition had names for these long before anyone had earbuds, and it never made them rivals. It made them a sequence. You read closely first, lectio, and only then could you ponder and rest in what you had read, contemplatio. Even the Gospel keeps the order. When the shepherds had gone and the noise died down, we are told that Mary “kept all these things, pondering them in her heart” (Lk 2:19). She received the event first. The pondering came after, and it was its own kind of knowing.

The younger technology

It is worth remembering that reading is the young technology here, not the old one. When writing first spread, the worry was a mirror image of ours: that committing thought to the page would hollow people out and leave us with men who seemed wise because they had read everything, but who knew nothing, having only borrowed other people’s thoughts and kept them as their own. For most of human history wisdom was carried by voice, argued in dialogue, held in the ear and the memory. The examined life that founded philosophy was never written down by the man who lived it.

So when depth begins to move back toward the ear, toward the slow turning-over of something heard, I am not convinced we are watching thought die. It may be changing address. The panic keeps mistaking a change of address for a death.

I have a whole career that quietly says as much. I sit with people for a living, and the deepest places I ever reach with another person, I do not reach by reading. I reach them by listening, by staying with what is half-said until it becomes whole. There is no page in the room. There is an enormous amount of thinking in it.

What actually goes missing

Here is the part I cannot leave out, because it is the true thing underneath all of it.

Contemplation needs something to contemplate.

My pondering at the gym is full because I spent years filling it. The reading, the arguing, the decades of listening closely to real people, all of it becomes the substance the open and contemplative mode has to work on. Take the substance away and the same posture produces nothing. You get the feeling of depth with an empty room behind it.

And that, not audio and not AI, is the real danger. The modern world is engineered to spare us all friction: the ninety-second video, the curated feed, the assistant that hands you the answer and then the judgment on top of it, here is what this means for you, here is what you should do next. That is not listening. It is being narrated to. It is the frictionless counterfeit of both faculties at once.

The variable was never reading against listening. It was friction against none. You can skim a book and touch nothing. You can carry a single sentence around a gym for a week and be changed by it. The feed is frictionless reading; the gym, for me, is friction-full listening. It is the same hinge I wrote about last week, whether you stay the author of your own thinking or quietly hand it over. The medium was only ever where the question happened to be standing.

What to keep in your hands

So I have stopped asking whether we are still a people who read. It is the wrong question, and it flatters the wrong virtue. The question underneath it is older and harder. It is whether we still bring anything to the silence. Whether, when the voice in the ear finally stops, there is a formed mind left to do the pondering, or only the pleasant hum of having been told.

Reading was never the point. It was one of the ways we filled the hands that contemplation needs.

Keep something in them.
